**Before running:** Ensure that `cleaned data.Rda` has been generated by running `cleaned_data.Rmd` and is saved in the same directory as this Rmd file.

**Viewing results:** Knit this file to HTML for easier viewing of formatted regression tables, equations and explanations. Individual code chunks can also be executed directly in RStudio.

# 1. Research objective and specification

We estimate the immigrant-sounding name penalty in employer callback rates and test whether it differs by three pre-specified moderators: language skills, extracurricular activities, and multinational firm experience. The regression estimates provide a theory-driven counterpart to the causal forest's subgroup treatment-effect estimates.

| Moderator (X) | Variable | Research question | Expected interaction |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Language skills | `language_skills` | Does listing language proficiency reduce the immigrant-name callback penalty? | Positive |
| Extracurricular activities | `extracurricular_skills` | Do extracurricular signals reduce the immigrant-name callback penalty? | Positive |
| Multinational firm experience | `same_exp` | Does multinational firm experience reduce the immigrant-name callback penalty? | Positive |

The regressions are estimated separately for each moderator, using the waves in which that characteristic was randomized. Language skills and extracurricular activities use Waves 0, 1 and 2, while multinational firm experience uses Waves 0 and 1 due to structural missingness in Wave 2.

All three regressions use a common control set comprising female, ba_quality, ma, and exp_highquality, alongside wave fixed effects. These controls are observed across all three waves, ensuring consistency in model specification across moderators. Standard errors are clustered by firmid using CR2.

# 2. Setup and data preparation

The analysis uses the cleaned Type 0/1 sample (`df_int1`) also used in the balance table and causal-forest scripts. Treatment `D = 1` indicates an immigrant-sounding name (Type 1), and `D = 0` an English-sounding name (Type 0). Outcome `callback` is binary. 

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
required <- c("dplyr", "estimatr", "knitr", "broom")
missing <- setdiff(required, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(missing)) install.packages(missing, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
library(dplyr)
library(estimatr)
library(knitr)
library(clubSandwich)
```

```{r load-data}
if (!file.exists("cleaned data.Rda")) {
  stop("Run cleaned_data.Rmd first, or put cleaned data.Rda in this working directory.")
}
loaded <- load("cleaned data.Rda")
stopifnot("df_int1" %in% loaded)
required_cols <- c("D", "callback", "firmid", "fall_data", "type",
                   "language_skills", "extracurricular_skills", "same_exp",
                   "female", "ba_quality", "ma", "exp_highquality")
stopifnot(all(required_cols %in% names(df_int1)))
dat <- df_int1 %>% mutate(
  D = as.numeric(as.character(D)),
  callback = as.numeric(as.character(callback)),
  wave = factor(fall_data)
)
stopifnot(all(na.omit(dat$D) %in% 0:1),
          all(na.omit(dat$callback) %in% 0:1))
cat("Observations:", nrow(dat), "\n")

#count under D = 0 and D = 1
print(table(dat$D, useNA = "ifany"))

#Firm count 
cat("Firms:", dplyr::n_distinct(dat$firmid), "\n")
```

The missingness-by-wave breakdown for the covariates is in the data-cleaning script. Based on those checks, we define a common set of controls consisting of covariates present across all three waves and construct moderator-specific estimation samples (only the same_exp regression is restricted to Waves 0 and 1).

```{r sample-definitions}
moderators <- c("language_skills", "extracurricular_skills", "same_exp")
moderator_waves <- list(
  language_skills = c(0, 1, 2),
  extracurricular_skills = c(0, 1, 2),
  same_exp = c(0, 1)
)

# Will be using common control set for all 3 interaction regressions with covariates observed across all three waves

common_controls <- c(
  "female",
  "ba_quality",
  "ma",
  "exp_highquality"
)

#define moderator-specific samples 

moderator_samples <- setNames(lapply(moderators, function(x) {
  dat %>%
    filter(fall_data %in% moderator_waves[[x]]) %>%
    mutate(wave = droplevels(wave))
}), moderators)

sample_summary <- bind_rows(lapply(moderators, function(x) {
  s <- moderator_samples[[x]]
  data.frame(moderator = x,
             waves = paste(moderator_waves[[x]], collapse = ", "),
             n = nrow(s),
             firm_clusters = n_distinct(s$firmid),
             n_x0 = sum(s[[x]] == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
             n_x1 = sum(s[[x]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE))
}))
kable(sample_summary, caption = "Moderator-specific estimation samples")
```

# 3. Baseline average treatment effect

We estimate the average immigrant-name treatment effect using a linear probability model with wave fixed effects and firm-clustered (CR2) standard errors. We report estimates with and without controls, using the same common control set as the ex-ante interaction regressions, to assess the sensitivity of the estimated treatment effect to their inclusion.

$$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \gamma' Z_i + \delta_t + \varepsilon_i$$

Here, $\beta_1$ represents the estimated average effect of an immigrant-sounding name on callback probability. $Z_i$ denotes the common control set, which is omitted in the specification without controls, while $\delta_t$ represents wave fixed effects. Standard errors are clustered by firmid using CR2.

```{r baseline-ate}
# Estimate wave-adjusted ATE
# ATE without controls (wave FE only)
ate_no_controls <- lm_robust(
  callback ~ D + wave,
  data = dat,
  clusters = firmid,
  se_type = "CR2"
)

# ATE with controls (common control set + wave FE)
ate_with_controls <- lm_robust(
  reformulate(c("D", common_controls, "wave"), response = "callback"),
  data = dat,
  clusters = firmid,
  se_type = "CR2"
)

# Extract treatment effect and inference statistics
ate_models <- list(
  "Without controls" = ate_no_controls,
  "With controls" = ate_with_controls
)

# Extract treatment effect and inference statistics

ate_table <- bind_rows(lapply(names(ate_models), function(nm) {
  fit <- ate_models[[nm]]

  results <- broom::tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
  treatment <- results[results$term == "D", ]

  data.frame(
    specification = nm,
    estimate = treatment$estimate,
    se = treatment$std.error,
    ci_low = treatment$conf.low,
    ci_high = treatment$conf.high,
    n = nobs(fit),
    firm_clusters = n_distinct(dat$firmid)
  )
}))

knitr::kable(
  ate_table,
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c(
    "Specification", "Treatment effect", "SE",
    "CI lower", "CI upper", "N", "Firm clusters"
  ),
  caption = "Average Immigrant-Name Treatment Effect With and Without Controls"
)
```
The estimated average treatment effect is −0.0443 without controls and −0.0442 with controls, indicating that resumes with immigrant sounding names receive approximately 4.4 percentage points fewer callbacks than those with English sounding names. Both estimates are statistically significant at the 5% level, with 95% confidence intervals excluding zero. There is negligible difference between the estimates with and without controls, suggesting that the estimated average name penalty is robust to the inclusion of controls.

Note: Our extension uses firm-clustered CR2 standard errors to account for potential dependence between multiple resumes submitted to the same employer. Unlike Oreopoulos (2011), which uses heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors, our approach accounts for potential within-firm correlation. This affects the standard errors but not the OLS point estimates for an otherwise identical specification.
```{r hc1-vs-cr2}
# Comparison bwt using HC1 and CR2
model_HC1 <- lm_robust(callback ~ D + wave, data = dat, se_type = "HC1")
model_CR2 <- lm_robust(callback ~ D + wave, data = dat,
                       clusters = firmid, se_type = "CR2")
data.frame(method = c("HC1", "CR2"),
           estimate = c(coef(model_HC1)["D"], coef(model_CR2)["D"]),
           SE = c(model_HC1$std.error["D"], model_CR2$std.error["D"]))
```

# 4. Three ex-ante interaction regressions

For each moderator $X$, we estimate the following linear probability model:

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 X_i + \beta_3(D_i \times X_i) + \gamma'Z_i + \delta_{w(i)} + \varepsilon_i
$$

The three regressions use a common set of controls including female, ba_quality, ma, and exp_highquality, alongside wave fixed effects. The estimation samples differ only for same_exp, which is restricted to Waves 0 and 1 due to structural missingness in Wave 2. Here, $\beta_1$ represents the immigrant-name effect when $X=0$, $\beta_2$ captures the effect of the moderator when $D=0$, and $\beta_3$ tests whether the immigrant-name effect differs between $X=1$ and $X=0$.

```{r fit-interactions}
# Estimate the three moderator-specific interaction regressions

fit_interaction <- function(x) {

  controls <- common_controls

  rhs <- c(
    "D",
    x,
    paste0("D:", x),
    controls,
    "wave"
  )

  f <- reformulate(rhs, response = "callback")

  lm_robust(
    f,
    data = moderator_samples[[x]],
    clusters = firmid,
    se_type = "CR2"
  )
}

models <- setNames(
  lapply(moderators, fit_interaction),
  moderators
)

sample_check <- data.frame(
  moderator = moderators,
  expected_n = unname(sapply(moderator_samples, nrow)),
  actual_n = unname(sapply(models, nobs))
)

sample_check$dropped <- sample_check$expected_n - sample_check$actual_n

knitr::kable(sample_check)

stopifnot(all(sample_check$dropped == 0))

```
This check verifies that the interaction regressions retain their intended sample sizes and that no additional observations are silently dropped by lm_robust() due to missing values in the controls.

```{r interaction-table}
# Extract interaction coefficients (beta_3) from each regression
interaction_table <- bind_rows(lapply(moderators, function(x) {

  m <- models[[x]]
  term <- paste0("D:", x)

  results <- broom::tidy(m, conf.int = TRUE)
  interaction <- results[results$term == term, ]

  if (nrow(interaction) != 1) {
    stop(paste("Interaction term not found:", term))
  }

  data.frame(
    moderator = x,
    beta3 = interaction$estimate,
    se = interaction$std.error,
    ci_low = interaction$conf.low,
    ci_high = interaction$conf.high,
    p_value = interaction$p.value,
    waves = paste(moderator_waves[[x]], collapse = ", "),
    n = nobs(m),
    firm_clusters = n_distinct(moderator_samples[[x]]$firmid)
  )
}))

knitr::kable(
  interaction_table,
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c(
    "Moderator", "β₃", "SE", "CI Lower", "CI Upper",
    "p-value", "Waves", "N", "Firm clusters"
  ),
  caption = "Ex-ante interaction regression results"
)
```

The results provide limited evidence of heterogeneity across the three pre-specified moderators. Language skills have a negative interaction coefficient (−0.0141), contrary to our hypothesis, but the estimate is not statistically significant (p = 0.4792). Extracurricular activities have a positive interaction coefficient (0.0311), suggesting a smaller immigrant-name penalty when extracurricular activities are listed. However, this effect is only significant at the 10% level (p = 0.0903). Multinational firm experience also has a positive interaction coefficient (0.0293), but the estimate is not statistically significant (p = 0.1837).

*Overall, none of the three interaction coefficients is statistically significant at the 5% level.* Hence, the ex-ante regressions do not provide strong evidence that these resume characteristics systematically moderate the immigrant-name penalty. The subsequent subgroup treatment-effect analysis examines the magnitude and uncertainty of the implied name penalty for X=0 and X=1.


Since treatment assignment is randomized, control variables are not required for identification but may improve precision. We assess the sensitivity of the interaction estimates to inclusion of controls by comparing β₃ across specifications with and without the common control set. Both specifications retain wave fixed effects and firm-clustered (CR2) standard errors.

```{r}

# Interaction regressions without additional controls
models_no_controls <- setNames(
  lapply(moderators, function(x) {
    lm_robust(
      reformulate(
        c("D", x, paste0("D:", x), "wave"),
        response = "callback"
      ),
      data = moderator_samples[[x]],
      clusters = firmid,
      se_type = "CR2"
    )
  }),
  moderators
)

# Compare interaction coefficients
robustness_table <- bind_rows(lapply(moderators, function(x) {
  term <- paste0("D:", x)

  data.frame(
    Moderator = x,
    Without_controls = unname(coef(models_no_controls[[x]])[term]),
    With_controls = unname(coef(models[[x]])[term])
  )
}))

robustness_table$Difference <- (
  robustness_table$With_controls - robustness_table$Without_controls
)

knitr::kable(
  robustness_table,
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c(
    "Moderator", "β₃ without controls",
    "β₃ with controls", "Difference"
  ),
  caption = "Robustness of Interaction Estimates to Controls"
)

```

The interaction coefficients change only slightly with the inclusion of controls (with the largest difference being 0.19 percentage points for language skills). This is consistent with the expectation that, under randomization, additional controls should primarily improve precision rather than significantly affect the estimated interaction effects.

# 5. Regression-implied subgroup treatment effects

For each binary moderator, the regression-implied subgroup treatment effects are:

$$
\hat{\tau}(X=0) = \hat{\beta}_1, \qquad
\hat{\tau}(X=1) = \hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3
$$

For $X=1$, the variance accounts for the covariance between $\hat{\beta}_1$ and $\hat{\beta}_3$:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3)
= \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)
+ \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3)
+ 2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_1,\hat{\beta}_3)
$$
In this code, subgroup treatment effects are obtained through an equivalent reparameterisation of the interaction regressions, allowing β₁ for X=0 and β₁ + β₃ for X=1 to be estimated directly, such that firm-clustered CR2 standard errors and confidence intervals can be calculated using lm_robust() without additional approximations.

```{r}
subgroup_effects <- bind_rows(lapply(moderators, function(x) {

  s <- moderator_samples[[x]]
  s$m <- s[[x]]
  s$m0 <- 1 - s$m

  # Reparameterise the original interaction regression: D:m0 = beta1 (X=0); D:m  = beta1 + beta3 (X=1)
  f <- reformulate(
    c("D:m0", "D:m", "m", common_controls, "wave"),
    response = "callback"
  )

  fit <- lm_robust(
    f,
    data = s,
    clusters = firmid,
    se_type = "CR2"
  )

  # Extract subgroup treatment effects and CR2 inference
  bind_rows(lapply(0:1, function(z) {

    term <- if (z == 0) "D:m0" else "D:m"

    data.frame(
      moderator = x,
      subgroup = paste0("X=", z),
      estimate = unname(coef(fit)[term]),
      se = unname(fit$std.error[term]),
      ci_low = unname(fit$conf.low[term]),
      ci_high = unname(fit$conf.high[term]),
      n_subgroup = sum(s$m == z),
      firm_clusters_subgroup = n_distinct(s$firmid[s$m == z])
    )
  }))
}))

knitr::kable(
  subgroup_effects,
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c(
    "Moderator", "Subgroup", "Treatment effect",
    "SE", "CI lower", "CI upper",
    "N", "Firm clusters"
  ),
  caption = "Estimated Immigrant-Name Treatment Effects by Subgroups"
)
```

The subgroup treatment effects represent the estimated immigrant-name penalty at X=0 (β₁) and X=1 (β₁ + β₃), with the difference between the two corresponding to the interaction coefficient β₃.

For language skills, the estimated name penalty increases from 4.06 to 5.48 percentage points when X = 1 (β₃ = −0.0141). The name penalty decreases from 6.30 to 3.19 percentage points for extracurricular activities (β₃ = 0.0311), and from 5.81 to 2.88 percentage points for multinational firm experience (β₃ = 0.0293). As earlier established, the differences in name penalty across subgroups (β₃) are all statistically insignificant. 


The subgroup treatment effects estimated from the interaction regressions will be compared with corresponding subgroup average treatment effects (ATEs) estimated using the causal forest. Both approaches will use the same subgroup definitions and target observations to ensure comparability. Specifically, the comparison for multinational firm experience will be restricted to Waves 0 and 1, while the other two moderators will use all three waves. The comparison will focus on the direction, magnitude and uncertainty of the estimated treatment effects.
